nicheStories.title: Navy retiring USS Fort Worth halfway through lifespan
nicheStories.description: This week, the Navy retired a littoral combat ship only halfway through its lifespan.The USS Fort Worth, a surface combatant ship which cost $400 million to build, entered service in 2012. It was originally meant to serve until the late 2030s, but was retired early due to chronic repair issues and related costs, and longstanding concerns regarding its overall viability.A major issue for the USS Fort Worth was its combining gear, which connects its gas turbine and engines to its water jet shafts. The combining gear took critical damage back in 2016 when crew members failed to follow proper procedures while testing its engines, rendering the boat functionally unusable. The Navy initially scheduled the USS Fort Worth’s retirement for 2022, after only ten years of service. However, the Navy repurposed the ship instead, using it to test new technologies at a port in San Diego.“By retiring early-hull test platforms like Fort Worth, the Navy redirects investments toward upgrading the remaining LCS inventory with enhanced capabilities,” the Navy said in a statement this week. Its retirement helps ensure “the active ships remain relevant, combat-credible, and reliable throughout their service lives.”But, as Dan Grazier, the director of the Stimson Center’s National Security reform program, tells RS: “The whole Littoral Combat Ship concept has failed.” “It's a poorly designed ship that [has an] excessive maintenance burden,” Grazier said. To Grazier’s point, a 2022 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found the Navy “hasn’t demonstrated that this type of ship can perform its intended missions,” and that it was less likely than its counterparts to withstand combat. The USS Fort Worth’s untimely demise is representative of a broader procurement crisis, where the Navy has repeatedly failed to deploy reliable ships that can perform their intended function. Rather, as Grazier tells RS, the Navy has often opted to build elaborately designed ships with unproven technologies, which often do not work as planned. “The Navy's now feeling the real consequences of years of bad policy,” Grazier said. “The size of the fleet is shrinking.”The Navy originally planned to buy 55 littoral combat ships; it cut back to 32 in 2014 as questions mounted about the program’s viability. It now has 27.

nicheStories.title: Trouble in Paris? There's a Gaullist cure for that American hubris
nicheStories.description: Last month, as world leaders prepared to gather in France for the G7 Summit, French officials had Donald Trump on the mind.Using its privileges as host, Paris worked diligently to avoid any hiccups that might upset the U.S. president. First, it delayed the meeting from June 14 to June 16, ensuring that it wouldn’t interfere with Trump’s 80th birthday celebration, or the cage match on the White House lawn that accompanied it. Then, French President Emmanuel Macron went “out of his way” to design an agenda to “appeal to the sort of things Trump wants,” as one analyst told Reuters.Last, and perhaps most bizarrely, French officials delayed the ceremonial transfer of the remains of French Resistance hero Marc Bloch, who was set to be reinterred at France’s illustrious Panthéon in the heart of Paris on June 16. This decision was consequential; it meant that, instead of carrying out the ceremony on the anniversary of Bloch’s murder by the Gestapo in 1944, officials had to pay tribute a week later, delaying a national tribute of exceptional historical significance for one of France’s greatest historians and patriots.In the end, France ultimately gave up honoring Marc Bloch on the very day of his martyrdom in order to adjust its schedule to the imperious wishes of the White House and, ultimately, to welcome the U.S. president to nearby Versailles in an effort to curry favor with him.These decisions reflect a sorry state of mind. Even when it comes to our own national history, France has grown accustomed to treating constraints originating in Washington as overriding priorities. Yet nothing required the ceremony to be postponed or the agenda to be reshaped. The relationship that should bind two great allied republics too often resembles one of political dependence, in which Paris is less concerned with defending its own interests and values than with deferentially anticipating Washington's wishes.This situation serves neither France nor the United States.A common misconception is that America's interests are best served by compliant allies who implement decisions made in Washington without question. That is the logic of empire, not of sovereign nations joined in partnership. The United States has far greater need of allies willing to speak candidly than of vassals eager to please, as recent history has repeatedly borne out.When Jacques Chirac's France refused to join the 2003 invasion of Iraq, it was accused of betraying the Western alliance. With the benefit of hindsight, who can seriously argue that Paris was wrong? No weapons of mass destruction were ever found, nor any relationship between Saddam Hussein and al-Qaida. The war shattered the Iraqi state, fueled the rise of jihadist terrorism, strengthened Iran's regional influence, and cost American taxpayers trillions of dollars – not to mention the vast number of American and Iraqi lives lost.France's refusal was undoubtedly unwelcome in Washington. Yet it proved salutary. It served as a vaccine against hubris – a timely reminder that no power, however great, is immune to error. It also echoed the enduring lesson of Thucydides' “History of the Peloponnesian War”: no democracy can ultimately prevail abroad while violating the very principles it claims to uphold.It was precisely this lesson that General de Gaulle understood when, in his 1966 Phnom Penh speech, he denounced the Vietnam War. He was not seeking to weaken the United States; he was trying to spare it a strategic disaster. He reminded Americans that no foreign army can indefinitely impose its will upon a people determined to shape its own destiny. History ultimately proved him right.This Gaullist tradition did not consist in systematically opposing Washington. It meant supporting the United States whenever shared interests converged — and saying no when it embarked on a dangerous course.It is precisely this capacity for independent judgment that has gradually disappeared.The Ukrainian crisis offers a striking example. At the 2008 NATO summit in Bucharest, French President Nicolas Sarkozy and German Chancellor Angela Merkel initially understood the risks. Both opposed extending the prospect of alliance membership to Ukraine and Georgia, knowing that Moscow regarded such a move as a strategic red line that risked triggering a major confrontation on the European continent.Had France firmly maintained that position and continued to promote a European security architecture encompassing Europeans, Russians, and Americans alike, the Ukrainian catastrophe might well have been avoided. Instead, Paris gradually abandoned this vision in favor of growing alignment with NATO enlargement and, inevitably, a logic of confrontation.The same mistake was repeated with NATO's missile defense system. By agreeing in 2012 to join a project purportedly aimed at Iran but viewed by Russia as a hostile strategic deployment, France helped fuel a new arms race. After President George W. Bush withdrew from the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, the priority should have been to rebuild strategic trust. Instead, we chose the opposite course.The same pattern emerged over Iran. When President Donald Trump unilaterally withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) in 2018, France should have firmly opposed the decision. It should have defended an agreement that was working, reduced the risk of war, and refused to force French companies out of Iran at Washington's behest. Once again, deference prevailed over independence. The successive crises that have engulfed the Middle East – and above all the recent war against Iran, which was interrupted, if only briefly, with the Memorandum of Understanding – have demonstrated the cost of that failure. The conflict ended in what many observers regard as a strategic setback for the United States, a conclusion reached by analysts as different as Robert Kagan in his widely discussed Atlantic essay "Checkmate in Iran" and John J. Mearsheimer.Even worse, should the recent resumption of hostilities evolve into a prolonged conflict, the consequences could extend far beyond the Middle East, triggering a severe global economic crisis in which Western economies would almost certainly bear the heaviest costs.The paradox is that this growing subordination by France, and Europe more generally, to the U.S. has not strengthened the transatlantic alliance; it has weakened it.A genuine alliance depends on partners capable of contributing distinct strengths. France possesses precisely such assets. It is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council. It has the world's second-largest maritime domain, an extensive diplomatic network, an independent nuclear deterrent, and a world-class strategic industrial base.In other words, France has all the attributes required to be an indispensable partner to the United States — provided that it rediscovers the confidence to act as itself.The world now taking shape is no longer that of the 1990s. The United States must increasingly shift its strategic resources toward the Indo-Pacific in response to China's rise. It will no longer be able — or willing — to shoulder the burden of Western security indefinitely. Its long-term interest therefore lies not in maintaining economic and cultural dependencies but in fostering allies that are more autonomous, more capable, and more willing to assume responsibility for their own security. France could play precisely this role.One fundamental truth must be restated: the United States is stronger when surrounded by free and sovereign partners. A Gaullist France — capable of offering support when circumstances require it and dissenting when necessary — would be far more valuable to America than a France preoccupied with securing Washington’s approval.The United States does not need a France that behaves as a supplicant. It needs a France willing to speak with candor — a France capable of reminding its ally that no great power remains truly great once it ceases to listen to its friends. By recovering the Gaullist spirit, France would not distance itself from America; it would once again become the ally America respects. Such a relationship would be more balanced, more effective, and better suited to the strategic realities of the twenty-first century – not a relationship of dependence, but an alliance between two sovereign republics united by a shared commitment to democracy and human freedom.

nicheStories.title: Will naming, shaming & sanctioning terror in Sudan stop bloodshed?
nicheStories.description: In June, a bipartisan group of senators introduced the Preventing External Aggression and Conflict Escalation (PEACE) in Sudan Act of 2026. In the House, the pending U.S. Engagement in Sudanese Peace Act and the RSF Terrorism Designation Act partly overlap with the PEACE Act. One of the most consequential questions raised by the various bills is whether to designate Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force that has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since 2023, as a terrorist group.What effects could a terrorist designation for the RSF have? Would a designation make ceasefire negotiations – being pursued, although amid much criticism, by President Donald Trump’s Africa advisor Massad Boulos – easier or more difficult? And would a designation constrain the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which is credibly accused of backing the RSF? To think through these issues, I talked with several experts on Sudan and on terrorism designations. The stakes go beyond Sudan. There are strong arguments for and against a designation. On the one hand, designating the RSF would index Washington’s commitment to stabilizing Sudan and ending a war that has killed tens of thousands, displaced millions and sent ripples throughout the Horn of Africa. The UAE already stands accused of pursuing a destabilizing and divisive foreign policy from Yemen to Sudan to Libya with its support for strongmen who fuel conflict. Targeting it could show Gulf monarchies that there are limits to their influence in Washington.On the other hand, sanctions regimes face increasing criticism, as their application from Iran to Russia have largely failed to produce sought-after behavior changes, have generally hardened the resolve of their targets, and resulted in unintended negative consequences for civilians. Terrorism designations can even make it harder for humanitarian relief agencies to operate due to fears they could be tarred as providing “material support.” The terrorism designations system has also been criticized as politicized and susceptible to executive overreach. In designating the RSF, a genocidal and destructive group by many standards, the U.S. might nevertheless reinforce problematic powers of the national security state.Moreover, several experts suggested that a designation will have little effect in isolation. If a designation is worth pursuing, it would need to be part of a broader strategy that the Trump administration has not, so far, articulated.Terrorism designations: Mechanisms and limitationsThe U.S. government has multiple designation mechanisms. The pending bills ask the secretary of state to apply the Specially Designated Global Terrorism (SDGT) mechanism. The SDGT designation can apply to a group or to an individual, and can be made by either State or Treasury, albeit under different parameters. The other main designation that might apply to the RSF – the Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) – can only be made by State. Both designation mechanisms apply financial sanctions, seeking to make it difficult for the designated entities to move money through the international banking system, as well as to hold property or other assets in the United States and elsewhere. The FTO designation is potentially more sweeping in that it criminalizes providing “material support” to a designated group. Meanwhile, the State Department maintains a list of State Sponsors of Terrorism, which included Sudan from 1993 to 2020.These designation mechanisms exist alongside other sanctions, including for Sudan. In January 2025, the outgoing Biden administration determined that “members of the RSF and allied militias have committed genocide in Sudan,” and sanctioned the RSF’s leader, Muhammad Hamdan Dagalo, known as “Hemedti.” However, the Sudanese journalist Eiad Husham told me that “targeted financial and personal sanctions have only a limited impact on the RSF leadership…many of them emerged from a regime that operated under international sanctions for nearly three decades, so they have experience adapting to those restrictions.” Husham added that “sanctions alone do not necessarily isolate individuals politically or diplomatically,” as evidenced by the visit of Hemedti’s brother Algoni to Washington in October 2025, despite being under sanctions himself.A terrorism designation for the RSF would not necessarily hinder the group. Jason Blazakis, a former State Department official who authored the recently published "Terror Disrupted: Countering the Financing of Terrorism," told me that enforcing terrorism designations overseas is difficult; the most effective applications involve “international cohesion” and broad coordination with other governments and the United Nations, something the Trump administration seldom seeks. Even with a coalition, enforcement would still be difficult: for example, Blazakis said, it is “very unlikely that RSF gold profits moving through the UAE would be flagged.” A recent UN report highlighted how a “war economy” fuels the conflict in Sudan; it would not be easy for a terrorism designation to disrupt flows of gum arabic and other commodities from Sudan.Possible political effectsEnforcement problems, however, would not necessarily render a designation meaningless. Blazakis commented that a designation could be wielded diplomatically as a stick now and as a carrot later. Washington leveraged the State Sponsors of Terrorism list for many years as a bargaining chip with Sudanese authorities in the past. To use a designation of the RSF as a tool for pressuring the UAE, as well as Ethiopia, Chad, Kenya, and other accused RSF supporters to break with the militia, according to Blazakis, would require considerable diplomatic finesse.For one expert on Sudan, Tufts University’s Alex de Waal, a designation would at least bring a greater degree of clarity to U.S. policy. Given that the U.S. government has deemed RSF guilty of genocide, de Waal told me, “It’s at least an oddity that being responsible for an exceptionally grave crime in international law seems to be inconsequential, but being designated a terrorist does have consequences.” Still, de Waal noted that “it would be difficult to designate an organization as a terrorist and then immediately talk to them.” The SAF, he added, aims for total military victory, and designating the RSF risked reinforcing the SAF’s “maximalist” position.The real target of a terrorist designation for the RSF is the UAE. Since war broke out in Sudan in 2023, substantial evidence has accumulated regarding Emirati logistical and material support to the RSF. Supply routes and foreign mercenaries have flowed through Chad, Somalia, Ethiopia, and Libya. Husham told me he does not expect the Trump administration to designate the RSF – but, if it did, the move “would force a difficult political and diplomatic conversation with Abu Dhabi.” If the UAE distanced itself from the RSF, that could weaken the group’s hold on western Sudan and even help bring an end to the war. While de Waal agreed that such a development would weaken the militia, it could also fracture it. “So while it’s hard enough to negotiate anything right now, it might be impossible if the RSF fractures.” What hope is there, finally, for a mediated settlement in Sudan? Cameron Hudson, a former U.S. diplomat and longtime Sudan watcher, has argued that designating the RSF could lead to a breakthrough with the SAF, which has rejected successive ceasefire proposals put forward by Boulos. Hudson has also argued, however, that “the latest round of U.S. sanctions on Sudan” – provoked by the alleged use by the SAF of chemical weapons – “will make getting the SAF to the ceasefire negotiation table even harder.” Husham is pessimistic about the Trump administration’s efforts. Boulos, Husham commented, “appears to be overseeing more than sixty countries while being short staffed and having no previous diplomatic experience. That is an enormous portfolio for anyone, particularly when dealing with a complex conflict like Sudan’s.”In short, a chain of events would have to occur before the RSF could be designated, much less for the designation to help end the war. In the meantime, the question of designating the RSF occasions reflection on whether and how the tools of the War on Terror can be used to make peace, disrupt networks of influence, and alter the politics of the Horn and the Gulf.

nicheStories.description: Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar (IITGN) and the Regional Centre for Biotechnology, Faridabad, have developed and tested a new class of fluorescent probes that enable scientists to visualize xylem, the specialized tissue responsible for transporting water and minerals through plants. The work, published in Plant and Cell Physiology, introduces a faster, more specific and sensitive staining method than conventional dyes, creating avenues to strengthen research on plant development, vascular biology and crop resilience.
